charts.title: Liquidity Risk
charts.sub: How tight US and global money conditions are, as a percentile of their own history (0 loose, 1 very tight)
charts.desc: Risk assets (stocks and crypto) tend to do best when money is loose and worst when it is tight. This score blends the 10-year real yield, the US dollar, credit spreads, money-supply (M2) growth and the Fed's net liquidity (balance sheet minus Treasury cash and reverse repos). High score = tight conditions, which are less supportive for risk assets.
charts.how: Five inputs from FRED, each turned into its own percentile (past only), averaged, then smoothed over 3 months. Needs at least 3 inputs available. Net liquidity growth uses WALCL minus TGA minus reverse repo.

charts.title: Credit Spread Risk
charts.sub: Moody's Baa corporate yield minus the 10-year Treasury, as a percentile of its own history
charts.desc: How much extra yield investors demand to hold risky company debt instead of government bonds. When that gap widens fast, lenders are getting nervous and credit is tightening, which has come before most recessions and many equity and crypto drawdowns. High score = spreads wide for their own history.
charts.how: Source: FRED BAA10Y (monthly average). Score = where the latest spread sits among every spread seen up to that month (0 = tightest ever, 1 = widest ever). No look-ahead.

charts.title: Yield Curve Recession Risk
charts.sub: US 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield; the flatter or more inverted, the higher the score
charts.desc: When short-term rates rise above long-term rates (an inverted curve) it has signalled a US recession ahead in every downturn since the 1970s, usually 6 to 18 months early. High score = curve inverted or very flat compared with its history.
charts.how: Source: FRED T10Y3M (monthly average). Score = percentile of the inverted spread (the more inverted, the higher). It is a warning gauge, not a timing tool.

charts.title: Bitcoin Risk
charts.sub: One 0 to 1 gauge of how stretched Bitcoin is, combining five valuation measures. You can change how much each counts.
charts.desc: Low scores have been where Bitcoin was cheap against its own history; high scores where it was stretched. It says where we are in the cycle, not what happens next. Use the sliders to remove or down-weight any measure and see how the score changes.
charts.how: Five measures, each turned into a percentile of its own past (no look-ahead) and smoothed over 7 days: price vs the 200-week average, price vs the log-regression trend, MVRV, MVRV Z-Score and the Puell Multiple. The score is their weighted average. Starts mid 2014 so there is enough history to rank.

charts.title: Logarithmic Regression
charts.sub: Bitcoin price with a long-term trend line and bands at ±1 and ±2 standard deviations (fitted on all data since 2011; slope 5.53)
charts.desc: A straight line fitted through Bitcoin's price on log scales shows its long-term growth path. The bands show how far price has historically swung from that path. Price near the bottom band has been cheap and near the top band stretched. Growth has been slowing over time, so older fits overstate the future.
charts.how: Least squares fit of ln(price) against ln(days since the genesis block, 3 Jan 2009), using daily prices from 2011. Bands are the standard deviation of the fit errors. This is fitted with hindsight on purpose: it is a map of the past, not a forecast.

charts.title: Puell Multiple
charts.sub: Daily value of newly mined bitcoin divided by its 365-day average
charts.desc: Miners sell much of what they earn, so the dollar value of new coins is a pulse on miner income. Very low readings (below about 0.5) have lined up with miner capitulation and major cycle lows. Very high readings (above about 4) have lined up with euphoric tops.
charts.how: Daily issuance (block reward from the halving schedule × 144 blocks) × price, divided by its 365-day average. Uses the reward only (not fees), as in the original definition. Halvings: Nov 2012, Jul 2016, May 2020, Apr 2024.
